abstract:
Portal vein tumor thrombus (PVTT) is the most common form of macrovascular invasion in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and is associated with poor prognosis, rapid intrahepatic dissemination, and limited responsiveness to systemic therapy. Increasing evidence indicates that PVTT is not merely an intravascular extension of the primary tumor, but rather a biologically distinct and highly adaptive immunosuppressive niche that contributes to immune escape and therapeutic resistance.
This review summarizes current genomic, transcriptomic, single-cell, and spatially resolved evidence regarding the immune landscape of PVTT in HCC. We discuss how early clonal divergence, hypoxia-associated metabolic rewiring, and stromal-vascular remodeling cooperatively shape the PVTT microenvironment. PVTT is characterized by enrichment of suppressive myeloid populations, activation of cancer-associated fibroblast programs, extracellular matrix accumulation, endothelial barriers to immune-cell trafficking, and progressive dysfunction or exclusion of effector lymphocytes. Together, these features establish a strongly immune-excluded and immunosuppressive ecosystem, providing a mechanistic basis for the limited efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade in patients with HCC-PVTT. We further highlight the translational implications of this framework for biomarker development, patient stratification, and rational combination strategies targeting suppressive myeloid and stromal programs, vascular barriers, and metabolic-immune crosstalk.
PVTT should be regarded as a distinct immunosuppressive niche rather than a passive vascular extension of the primary tumor. Its immune landscape is shaped by coordinated interactions among tumor evolution, metabolic adaptation, stromal remodeling, and immune dysfunction. A better mechanistic understanding of PVTT may support biomarker-guided stratification and the development of more effective precision therapies for HCC with macrovascular invasion.

Cancer</MedlineTA><NlmUniqueID>101597993</NlmUniqueID><ISSNLinking>1664-5553</ISSNLinking></MedlineJournalInfo><OtherAbstract Type="plain-language-summary" Language="eng"><AbstractText>Portal vein tumor thrombus (PVTT) happens when liver cancer grows into the portal vein, a major blood vessel of the liver. In hepatocellular carcinoma, PVTT is linked to faster disease spread, worse liver function, and poorer survival. Patients with PVTT also often benefit less from immunotherapy, which is a treatment that helps the immune system attack cancer. This review explains why PVTT may be harder to treat than the main liver tumor. We describe evidence showing that PVTT is not just an extension of the original tumor. Instead, it seems to behave like a separate cancer-supporting environment. In this environment, cancer cells can change their metabolism, build physical barriers around themselves, and interact with nearby supportive cells in ways that weaken the body’s immune response. As a result, immune cells may have trouble entering the tumor area or may become less effective even if they do reach it. We also summarize how these findings may help with future treatment. A better understanding of PVTT could support the development of better biomarkers, improve patient selection for therapy, and guide combination treatments that target not only cancer cells but also the surrounding immune-suppressive environment.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>© The Author(s) 2026.
